name: Omar Santos

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Omar. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Amina and I own Ridgeback Farm, a hundred and ten hectares of hill ground. We run five hundred ewes and thirty suckler cows, and we cut our own hay in July. I've got an apprentice, Callum, who's nineteen and keen. In early summer I'm away four days a week with a shearing gang, which pays very well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What does a normal day look like out of shearing season?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Up at six, round the ewes on the quad with the dog, feeding the cows, fixing walls. Callum and I eat our sandwiches in the Land Rover and argue about football. In the evening I sometimes ask the AI on my phone about the weather or lamb prices, but only now and then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've always said: hard work and good stock beat any gadget. I'd tell the lads at the market that the clever stuff is fine for forms, and that's where it stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means things carry on, and that's good for us. The land is paid for, the lambs are selling well, and a nineteen-year-old apprentice is learning what my father taught me. I'd be content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep the flock and the cows as they are. Keep Callum on and get him through his college certificate next year. Maybe use the phone AI a bit more for checking the weather before haymaking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Grateful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything already pressing on you, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My knees, after thirty-five years of shearing. And the wool's worth nothing, but the lambs make up for it. Nothing that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why does the apprentice matter so much to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because someone taught me. Old Mr Hughes took me on at sixteen and never charged me a penny for what I learned. I owe that forward.

say: Hard work and **good stock** beat any gadget.
The clever stuff is fine for **forms**, and that's where it stays.
think: The land is **paid for** and the lambs sell **well**.
His **apprentice** is learning what his father taught him.
do: Keep the **flock and cows** as they are.
Get **Callum** through his college certificate next year.
Use the phone AI a bit more for **haymaking weather**.
S0.quote: The land is paid for, the lambs are selling well, and a nineteen-year-old apprentice is learning what my father taught me.
fieldNote: Owns the land outright, lamb prices are good: his calm is **earned**.
Values **apprenticeship** as a debt he owes forward.
Uses AI **now and then**, mainly for weather and prices.

steps.text: Keep the 500 ewes and 30 suckler cows as they are
Get apprentice Callum through his college certificate next year
Use the phone AI to check weather before haymaking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's got a head start, because you can't email a sheep. I'd also tell the young ones to learn a trade with their hands, not just a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my own work barely changes. A computer can write the sheep movement forms, but it can't teach my apprentice Callum how to catch a ewe. The worry is Callum's generation, and my daughter Leila, who teaches, because marking and planning are thinking work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the AI do the sheep movement forms and the subsidy claim, now it's proven, and save myself a wet Sunday. I'd keep Callum on and teach him the stock work properly. And I'd talk to the young farmers' club about apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy for the young ones, steady for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your daughter Leila?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my daughter Leila to be the teacher the children remember, because a computer can mark homework but it can't sit with a crying child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would this change the farm's money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. If anything, the forms get cheaper and I save the accountant a few hours. The lambs sell at the same mart.

say: Farming has **a head start**, because you can't email a **sheep**.
Young people should learn a **trade** with their hands.
think: His own work **barely changes** in Steady Disruption.
He worries for **Callum's generation** and his daughter **Leila**, a teacher.
do: Let AI do the **movement forms** and subsidy claim.
Talk to the young farmers' club about **apprenticeships**.
feel: **Steady** for himself, **uneasy** for the young ones.
S1.quote: A computer can write the sheep movement forms, but it can't teach my apprentice Callum how to catch a ewe.
fieldNote: Mostly **hands-on** work, so his day changes little.
Adopts AI for **forms** now that it's proven: steady, not eager.
Worry is about the **next generation**: his apprentice and his teacher daughter.

steps.text: Let the AI fill in sheep movement forms and the subsidy claim
Teach Callum the stock work properly
Push apprenticeships at the young farmers' club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people need to look after their own and keep working, not wait for the government to save them. I'd also say that families and communities will matter more than ever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it worries me more than I'd say at the mart. Shearing money pays for our winter, and a shearing robot in 2031 would take it the summer I turn sixty-three. The big lowland farms would get robot shepherds too, and lamb prices would slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put every penny of this year's shearing money into savings, instead of the new quad. I'd cut back on the cows, maybe sell ten, so the farm runs on less. And I'd sit down with Amina and our daughters about whether Callum should stay, or whether I'd be doing him a disservice keeping him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. The land's safe, but the money on top of it isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between thinking AI and robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the forms and the prices get done by computers, which suits me. The trouble is 2031, when the shearing robots come. Three years is long enough to save, but not long enough to replace that money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd question keeping Callum on. What would you tell him?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Callum the truth: learn the stock, but learn to fix the robots too, because that's where the wages will be. It would break my heart to say it.

say: People should look after **their own** and **keep working**, not wait for rescue.
**Families and communities** will matter more than ever in hard times.
think: A **shearing robot** in 2031 would take his summer income at sixty-three.
Robot shepherds on lowland farms would push **lamb prices** down.
do: Save **all the shearing money** this year instead of buying a quad.
Sell **ten cows** so the farm runs on less.
Talk with Amina and the daughters about **Callum's future**.
feel: **Anxious**: the land's safe, but the **money on top** isn't.
S2.quote: Shearing money pays for our winter, and a shearing robot in 2031 would take it the summer I turn sixty-three.
fieldNote: The three-year gap gives him **time to save**, not to replace income.
His **shearing income** and lamb price are both at risk.
Torn over his **apprentice**, whom he'd steer towards fixing robots.

steps.text: Save all of this summer's shearing money instead of buying a quad
Sell ten of the thirty suckler cows
Steer apprentice Callum towards learning to fix robots

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning and people should get on with it, not moan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is long enough to see whether the robots actually work on a wet hill. The robots come in 2034, when I'm sixty-six and ready to hang up the shears anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep shearing while my knees hold, and save the money. I'd wait for the first robots to be tested by others, then maybe buy a second-hand one for the hay in 2035. And I'd get Callum on a robotics short course at the college, paid by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but all right. It feels like enough time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever buy a robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once I've seen one work on a neighbour's hill for a year, yes. Not the first model. Never the first model.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why pay for Callum's course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Hughes would have. And because a lad who can do both, stock and machines, will never be out of work.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, so get on with it, **not moan**.
think: He'll see whether robots work on a **wet hill**.
Robots in **2034** come when he's ready to stop shearing anyway.
do: Keep **shearing** while his knees hold and **save** the money.
Buy a **second-hand robot** for hay around 2035, once proven.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to see whether the robots actually work on a wet hill.
fieldNote: Five years lines up the robots with his **retirement from shearing**.
Classic steady adopter: **never the first model**.
Invests in his **apprentice** as Mr Hughes once did in him.

steps.text: Keep shearing while his knees hold and bank the money
Buy a second-hand hay robot once neighbours have proven it
Pay for Callum's robotics short course at the college

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and there's no excuse not to be ready. Work hard, train the young ones and look after your neighbours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's comfortable. When robots reach the hills in 2039, I'll be sitting at the gate telling my apprentice Callum how we used to do it. The farm will go to Callum on a tenancy, or one of the girls' children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as I am. Train Callum, keep the flock, slow down on the shearing from sixty-two. Wait and see what the robots look like before I make any choice about the farm's future.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Content, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you worry here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the young ones don't use the time. Ten years goes quickly, and I've seen lads waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the farm to look like in 2040?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sheep on the hill, a young farmer, and maybe a robot carrying the bales. I could live with that.

say: Ten years is **plenty**, so there's **no excuse** not to be ready.
Work hard, **train the young**, and look after your neighbours.
think: Robots reach the hills in **2039**, after his working years.
The farm may pass to **Callum** on a tenancy, or a grandchild.
do: Keep training **Callum** and keep the flock.
**Wait and see** before deciding the farm's future.
S4.quote: When robots reach the hills in 2039, I'll be sitting at the gate telling my apprentice Callum how we used to do it.
fieldNote: A decade puts robots **beyond his working years**.
His only fear is young people **wasting the time**.
Already pictures **Callum** as the farm's next keeper.

steps.text: Keep training Callum and running the flock
Wait to see the robots before deciding who gets the farm

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the shearing money goes just before I'd stop anyway, and lamb prices slide. What would help is apprenticeships that teach the young ones both the stock and the machines, paid for by the industry, not handouts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the apprentice. I'd say: when you're my age, the job you care about most is the one you pass on. Every farmer my age should be training someone, robots or no robots.

headlineQuote: When you're my age, the job you care about most is the one you pass on.
portrait: Omar, **58**, owns a hill sheep and cattle farm and earns extra in a **shearing gang**.
He trains a **nineteen-year-old apprentice**, repaying the man who trained him.
He uses AI **now and then** and adopts tools only once proven.
Fast AGI threatens his **shearing income** and lamb prices; he saves and slims down.
With more time he stays **calm**, focused on passing the farm on.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because the shearing money and lamb **prices** fall before he stops.
whatWouldHelp: **Industry-paid apprenticeships** teaching both stock and machines.
